data.title: Price of diesel hits all-time high as wars in Iran, Ukraine constrict global supply
data.description: The price of diesel fuel hit an all-time high Friday as wars on two continents and a global refinery shortage combined with higher seasonal demand to push prices upward. The average nationwide price was $5.85 per gallon, up from $5.78 on Thursday, according to AAA’s gas price tracker. Diesel prices began their monthslong rise in late February, with the launch of the Iran war and the soaring oil prices that came with it. More recently, however, those rising prices have been sustained by an escalation in the fourth year of the war between Russia and Ukraine. Russia has long been the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel fuel after the United States. But Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s oil refineries have cut into the country’s diesel production. Facing a potential domestic supply shortage, Russia recently extended a diesel export ban through the end of September, straining what were already critically low global diesel reserves. Russia’s abrupt exit from the world’s diesel export market has been a boon, however, for U.S. refiners, whose diesel products now fetch even higher prices. America’s total diesel exports hit an all-time high last month as the world scrambled to adjust to the loss of Russia’s supply. Diesel also faces higher seasonal demand that is compounding the effects of the supply shortages. Around the world, farmers rely on diesel fuel to power the machines they use for both harvesting and planting. Meanwhile, colder temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere will also create higher demand for refined distillate fuels — the energy category that includes diesel. Taken together, those forces are increasingly putting diesel prices on a path apart from the rest of the global oil markets. For U.S. consumers, high diesel prices are likely to translate into higher costs for virtually any goods they purchase. Diesel powers most major freight transport, from boats to trains to trucks, and those higher input costs are eventually passed along in retail prices, in part or entirely. “It’s highly likely that transportation companies are not going to be able to absorb 100% of these cost increases,” said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM U.S. management consulting company. “Consumers should be prepared to pay higher inflation for anything that requires being shipped,” he said. The cost of groceries is likely to be especially hard hit, Brusuelas said, because many supermarkets are already operating on razor-thin margins because of the rising cost of beef. The latest diesel fuel cost increases could also reverse a trend of stabilizing inflation rates for food at home in recent months. Diesel fuel products are also used to heat homes across the U.S., and the price surges threaten to increase electricity costs when many households are already stretching their budgets to keep up with soaring utility bills. On Tuesday, President Donald Trump pressed oil refiners at a gathering at the White House about ways they could relieve the cost burden on end consumers. “This was not a ‘drill, baby, drill’ meeting,” White House deputy press secretary Taylor Rogers said. “This was a ‘refine, baby, refine’ meeting.” It was unclear Friday whether the companies had made any concrete commitments to increase refinery output that is already near capacity. But the issue of rising fuel costs is becoming an increasingly urgent one for the White House. Trump faces growing voter anxiety over the state of the U.S. economy, especially affordability issues, as November’s midterm elections loom.

data.title: Oil touches $97 per barrel as diesel prices surge to highest level this year
data.description: The price of crude oil rose for a fourth straight trading session on Thursday, part of a monthlong run that has helped push the average cost of diesel fuel to its highest level since 2022. At $5.78 per gallon on Thursday morning, the cost of diesel is up more than 53% since the war with Iran started in late February. At the time, diesel averaged $3.76 per gallon nationwide. The price of unleaded gasoline, which most personal vehicles run on, rose alongside diesel Thursday. According to AAA data tracked by NBC News, the national average was $4.14 per gallon, up two cents from Wednesday. The moves higher in retail fuel prices come as crude oil prices keep climbing. After surpassing $97 per barrel Thursday morning, international oil benchmark Brent was now up almost 10% since the beginning of the week. But experts are especially focused this week on diesel, the fuel powers everything from boats and trains to farm equipment and 18-wheelers. Around the world, the planting and harvesting of crops are dependent on diesel-powered machines. As a result, higher diesel prices now could mean higher grocery prices later this fall. Several different factors are fueling the global rise in energy prices. Chief among them is the ongoing war in Iran, which analysts view as a stalemate that has choked major maritime arteries for oil and gas. Recent attacks on ships in the critical Strait of Hormuz, coupled with retaliatory U.S. strikes on Iranian targets, mean that daily vessel traffic in the waterway remains minimal. Before the war, the strait was a critical passageway through which about 20% of the world’s oil supply passed to reach ports around the globe. Also putting pressure on gas prices this week is the recent escalation of the Ukraine war. “Following Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries, Russia has banned diesel exports until the end of September amid domestic supply concerns,” wrote ING commodities analysts. “This matters because Russia is the world’s second-largest diesel exporter. Combined disruptions are equivalent to around 20% of global seaborne diesel trade.” Only two developments could realistically be expected to bring meaningful relief to oil and gas prices, they wrote. One is a higher flow of oil and gas through the Persian Gulf, and the other is a resumption of Russian exports. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump said the latest round of U.S. strikes on Iran would not last “too long,” but he added, “We’re prepared to do another one any time we want.” He also said U.S. forces were “bringing lots of boats out” of the Strait of Hormuz each day. The president’s upbeat comments did little to ease oil price pressures, however. Last week, Goldman Sachs Research estimated that Persian Gulf oil exports have recovered to about two-thirds of pre-war levels. On Thursday, ING estimated it was about 50%. But those figures, likewise, brought little comfort to energy markets. Wholesale gas prices were up 1% in early Thursday trading, as was natural gas. One of the many knock-on effects of the energy price shock has been a broad expectation among investors that inflation will stay elevated. This in turn has driven up U.S. Treasury yields, which are sensitive to inflation projections. After climbing all week, bond yields finally dipped slightly on Thursday as markets weighed the odds of an interest rate hike later this month. That small drop is unlikely to bring any relief to consumers, however. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate hit 6.91% late Wednesday. Still, despite the rising energy prices and protracted wars, Federal Reserve governor Christoper Waller said Thursday that he expects consumer and wholesale inflation readings in the weeks ahead to be “reasonable,” which in Fed-speak means not-too-high. From Waller’s viewpoint, “So far energy [prices have] not bled into other goods and prices.” That said, if inflation data for August “Comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike,” he said at an event hosted by the Reuters news agency. ”I’m going to paraphrase John Lennon here,” said Waller. “Give disinflation a chance.”

data.title: Tracking U.S., state and county gas prices, in maps and charts
data.description: The war in Iran has led to higher prices at the gas pump. Gas prices in the United States, up by more than 30% since the U.S. and Israel launched the war, have soared as the global oil supply constricts. Now at a national average of close to $4 per gallon, according to data from motor club AAA, this price increase is straining already-stretched budgets in households across the country. NBC News is tracking gas prices and how they change at the national, state and county levels, and will be updating this article daily with the latest data. Average gas prices have increased more than a dollar since the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran. In three states — California, Hawaii and Washington — average gas prices are at more than $5 per gallon. Indiana, Mississippi and Texas are paying the least, according to AAA data. According to a Brown University analysis, the increase in gas prices since the start of the war has cost Americans more than $50 billion. Fuel costs aren’t limited to gas. Jet fuel prices have been surging as well, leading airlines to increase airfares and pressing Spirit Airlines to shutter. Oil prices have spiked, then see-sawed, and are approaching pre-war levels as turmoil in the Middle East continues. Since mid-May, the average national gas price has dropped around 40 cents. The average price is still up more than a dollar per gallon since the start of the war.

data.title: Gas cost calculator: How much have higher gas prices cost you?
data.description: After more than four months of war, does your wallet feel lighter? Since the Iran war started, Americans have spent an additional $50 billion on gasoline, according to a Brown University estimate. Increased gas prices have resulted in higher monthly expenses for individuals — anywhere from less than $20 to more than $300 for a driver who fills up twice a month, according to an NBC News analysis of motor club AAA’s average national gas price data. Just how much has the spike in gas prices bitten into your budget? Use our calculator to estimate your additional expenses at the pump since the start of the war. The calculator updates with the latest data daily. The cost model used in the calculator uses a sample of the average daily gas price in the United States since the start of the war, simulating how gas prices vary depending on which day you fuel up. The results you get will fall in a range of average costs and change slightly as you use the tool. Since Feb. 28, when the U.S. and Israel first struck Iran, average gas prices nationally have risen more than 30%. U.S. gas prices in early May were among the most expensive those prices had been in the past decade at an average of $4.63 per gallon, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The average gas price last topped $4 in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine. Faced with higher prices, some Americans are driving less, or at least filling up less often. An analysis by the location analytics company Placer.ai found gas station visits across the U.S. were down 5.7% the week of May 18, compared with the corresponding week in May 2025. At the state level, an NBC News analysis finds Utah residents are feeling the greatest strain since the start of the war, with gas prices up about 50% since February, averaging $4.30 per gallon as of early August. Montana and Wisconsin, in addition to Utah, have experienced the highest rates of change, with prices up about 50% from five months ago. Washington state’s gas prices have remained the most resilient, up less than 20% — about 75 cents — since February. To alleviate pain at the pump, some states have paused their gas taxes or postponed increases. Members of the Trump administration discussed pausing the federal gas tax, but they have yet to act on the initiative. Methodology This is how the NBC News gas cost calculator estimates the added costs: The calculator inputs the number of gallons in a refueling and the number of fill-ups per month, as provided by the reader, as well as average daily national gas prices from Feb. 28 to today.Based on the number of fill-ups, particular days’ per-gallon prices are sampled, reflecting how often a person may be going to the pump (every 10 days, 15 days, 30 days, etc.).The extra costs are calculated by subtracting the Feb. 28 per-gallon price from the average of the sampled prices. The result is then multiplied by the number of fill-ups and multiplied again by the number of gallons in the gas tank. Data is sourced from AAA’s daily posted national gas price averages and dates to Feb. 28. It updates with new daily numbers each morning.

data.title: The sardine shortage is real — and it’s not all Gen Z’s fault
data.description: Where are the sardines? The humble little fish, once a plentiful, budget-friendly staple in your grandpa’s pantry, can sometimes be hard to find. Sardines have become so celebrated by wellness influencers on TikTok, demand has skyrocketed, causing the oily nutritional powerhouses to go missing from grocery shelves. Becca Millstein, the CEO and co-founder of Fishwife, a hip Los Angeles-based tinned seafood company that launched in 2020, said the sardine supply chain is “tight” for multiple reasons. Warmer ocean temperatures in the mid-Atlantic are causing sardines to “migrate to deeper, cooler waters that are outside the typical range of commercial fishing nets,” Millstein said via email. Ocean temperatures also contribute to fluctuations in the growth of sardines’ favorite food source: phytoplankton. The fish aren’t growing as big as they should and reproduction rates are down, a 2025 study by marine researchers at the University of Barcelona found. A decline in catches in Morocco, the world’s leading exporter of canned sardines, eventually led the country to ban exports early this year to prioritize its domestic supply, according to Reuters. The ban cut off the supply to canneries in Spain and Portugal, which, along with Morocco, manufacture many canned sardines sold in the United States. “Because the global market relies heavily on those specific exports, the industry felt the impact very quickly,” said Millstein. The rise of #sardinemaxxing TikTok wellness influencers began touting sardines as a cheap, nutrient-dense, shelf-stable food during the early days of the Covid pandemic. Then Gen Zers and millennials embraced the unglamorous pantry staple of our grandparents with viral #sardinegirldinner videos, leading up to this year’s #sardinemaxxing trend. No wonder tinned sardine lovers are griping on Reddit about their favorite brands vanishing from grocers’ shelves. Some report shelling out more money than usual upon discovering the brands back in stock. Sardines are high in protein, omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin B12 and essential minerals like phosphorus and selenium. Because they’re eaten soft bones and all, they are also rich sources of calcium and vitamin D. “The long-chain omega-3s, EPA and DHA, which are in fatty fish, have been shown to have potential benefits for a range of tissues and organs,” said Dr. Dariush Mozaffarian, a cardiologist and the director of the Food Is Medicine Institute at Tufts University. National grocery chains say they’re trying to keep the sardines in stock. “Like the rest of the industry, we’ve seen shifts in sardine availability alongside growing consumer interest,” said AnaMaria Friede, the grocery director at Whole Foods Market. “Our sourcing team has been proactively partnering with suppliers to secure inventory, and we’re confident customers will see strong availability heading into fall.” Maria Brous, the director of communications at Publix Super Markets, said the availability of tinned sardines, as with other seafood products, is “influenced by a variety of factors” that include “fishing regulations, environmental conditions, import volumes, and overall market trends.” Amanda Chen, the senior brand manager for tinned seafood company King Oscar, said its inventory squeeze is due to consumer demand, not fewer fish. The brand, founded in 1902, is beloved by the #sardinecore set and sources seafood from Morocco — but not its signature Norwegian brisling sardines. Those smaller sardines are “wild caught in pristine, icy Nordic and Baltic waters, just as we’ve been doing for the last 124 years,” Chen said in an email. “We have seen category consumption growth in the range of 25% to 50% year over year across the various types of products. It is causing industry-wide constraints, mostly related to operational capacity and the timing of the fishing seasons rather than the fish supply itself,” Chen said. Beyond Morocco, sardines are caught in the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of northern Spain, the Baltic Sea and Sweden’s North Atlantic coast. When will sardine lovers see more stock? The good news is the situation is expected to get better. King Oscar is “working hard” to improve its inventory “as quickly as possible so consumers can find their favorite sardines once again,” said Chen. “We expect to fully recover in 2027,” Chen added. Millstein at Fishwife said her company will continue working with a “rotating portfolio of sustainable fisheries across different hemispheres” and multiple canneries in an effort to navigate environmental shifts and build long-term resilience in its supply chain. Millstein said she’s optimistic about the future of the fish. “A temporary shortage of fish on the market is often evidence that sustainability guardrails, like strict scientific quotas, are functioning exactly as intended to prevent long-term depletion.”

data.title: Map: See how gas prices have changed in the county where you live
data.description: Gas prices are up across the country, but nowhere are they up as much as in Johnson County, Wyo., where an average gallon of gas would run you $4.37 a gallon Friday, 70% more than the price at the start of the Iran war. How much gas prices have increased depends on where you live, an NBC News analysis of average gas price data from AAA shows. Johnson County’s price was up $1.81 a gallon, while Fisher County, Texas, population 3,600, prices had only increased 51 cents as of Friday. It also depends on the state. In Indiana, average gas prices are up $0.78 per gallon, among the lowest state-level increases in the nation (Indiana has repeatedly suspended its state gas tax). But in Montana, the average price is up $1.52 per gallon, the largest state-level increase in the U.S. This map, showing the latest county-level gas prices and the change in prices since the start of the war, will be updated daily. Polling consistently indicates that prices and the economy rank among voters’ top issues ahead of the midterm elections. An April poll showed gas prices were a problem for nearly two-thirds of Americans. As of early May, counties have seen increases of an average of $1.47 per gallon. However, about 100 counties, mostly in Indiana and Ohio, have seen price increases of $2 per gallon or more. Conversely, a little more than a dozen counties — mostly in Georgia and Nebraska — have seen price increases of less than $1 per gallon. See the trends of gas prices nationally and on the state level with the NBC News gas price tracker, and calculate how much the gas price increase has cost you with the the NBC News gas cost calculator.

data.title: Trump’s new Fed chair walks fine line on inflation in key speech
data.description: JACKSON HOLE, Wyo. — President Donald Trump’s new Federal Reserve Chair said Friday that although measures of inflation are still elevated, it is not yet clear that the central bank must take urgent action to address rising prices. The speech at the Fed’s yearly retreat to Jackson Hole, Wyoming, had been eagerly anticipated after a rocky start to Warsh’s tenure. Market observers were concerned that Warsh had downplayed the risk of rising prices. There were also calls for an interest rate from economists, including some within the Fed. Trump has routinely called for lower rates that would spark the economy but risk even greater inflation. Warsh noted that the labor market looks “stable,” and said this was one reason that he saw prices as “more concerning.” The Fed chairman noted that while readings of inflation this summer were “better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” Warsh did not say how the Fed would react if prices keep rising at rates above the target of 2%. But he underscored that the chief tool for tackling inflation was rate hikes. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do,” Warsh said. Following Warsh’s speech, the odds that the Fed would raise its benchmark interest rate next month in order to cool inflation increased. Warsh reiterated his preference for a “quieter Fed,” doing away with his predecessor’s use of “forward guidance” to let markets and the general public know what the central bank planned to do in the near future. “If markets rely materially on the Fed’s guidance and the Fed relies on market prices, we are all more likely to be blinded to new developments, more likely to be caught unprepared for a turn of events, and more likely to commit errors in policymaking,” Warsh said.

data.title: Map: How much you pay in federal and state gas taxes
data.description: As national gas price averages tick up, multiple states have suspended or reduced their gas taxes, and President Donald Trump and his Cabinet have talked about doing the same. While a suspension would offer some relief, an NBC News analysis shows that gas prices would still average 14% more per gallon than they were at the start of the Iran war, even if all state and federal taxes were suspended. Average gas prices nationwide are up more than 30% since the war was launched at the end of February. Trump told reporters in May that he intended to suspend the 18 cents per gallon federal gas tax. Such a suspension would require an act of Congress. Democrats in the House and Senate proposed measures to suspend the gas tax in March. “All measures that can be taken to lower the price at the pump and lower the prices for Americans, this administration is in support of,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” in May. An average of 52 cents in taxes and fees is tacked onto every gallon of regular gas that’s pumped in America. Some of this revenue goes to the state levying the tax, and about 18 cents of it goes to the federal coffers. Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky and Utah have each made modifications to their gas tax since prices started climbing: Georgia’s gas tax was suspended from March to early June.Illinois put a six-month pause on a 7-cent gas tax increase scheduled to go into effect July 1.Indiana’s gas tax holiday was extended through to early August, then extended again to early September.Kentucky’s statewide gas tax reduction expired near the beginning of June.Utah reduced its gas tax from 37.9 cents to 31.9 cents, on regular gas only. How much these taxes and fees account for varies: 6.7% of Hawaii’s cost per gallon goes to taxes and fees, while 20.9% of the price people in Illinois pay comes from state and federal taxes and fees, according to an NBC News analysis. On average, across all states, 13.5% of the price paid per gallon goes to taxes and fees as of July. Taxes and fees range from 27 cents per gallon in Alaska to 89 cents per gallon in California. Note that local taxes are not factored into this data. Some of the federal gas tax money goes toward the Highway Trust Fund, which itself is used to fund highway and mass transit projects. One estimate put the cost of a gas tax holiday at a minimum of $2.5 billion per month. In March, Trump said at a Cabinet meeting that he had “thought about” suspending the federal gas tax. The federal gas tax has not been increased since Bill Clinton signed the last increase into law in 1993. The 18 cents it cost per gallon in 1993, after inflation, would be worth 8 cents in 2026 dollars. CORRECTION (May 14, 2026, 3:15 p.m. ET): A previous version of a chart and map in this article miscalculated Indiana’s and Utah’s average price per gallon of gas without state taxes. The state taxes had already been removed or reduced from the current price, which the graphics did not acknowledge.

data.title: Lucky Charms and Trix go au naturel as General Mills ditches artificial colors
data.description: General Mills said Wednesday it has removed artificial colors from all its U.S. cereals, including Lucky Charms and Trix. The Minneapolis company has shifted to fruit- and vegetable-based dyes as well as colors derived from spices like turmeric and paprika to give its cereals their customary bright colors. “This achievement reflects how we are evolving with consumer needs while continuing to offer food that tastes great, delivers quality and provides value,” said Bethany Quam, General Mills’ president of cereal, in a statement. General Mills said 90% of its U.S. retail products are now free of artificial dyes. Products that still contain artificial colors, like some Betty Crocker cake mixes and Fruit Roll-Ups, will transition to natural dyes by the end of 2027, the company said. General Mills is the second big cereal maker to announce a transition to natural dyes. WK Kellogg, which makes Froot Loops and Apple Jacks, said earlier this month that it will remove artificial colors from all its U.S. cereals by the end of this year. Health advocates have long called for the removal of artificial dyes from foods, citing studies indicating they can cause neurobehavioral problems, including hyperactivity and attention issues, in some children, though the findings have been mixed. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says approved dyes are safe and that “most children have no adverse effects” from them. But the agency says some children may be sensitive to artificial dyes. Last year, the FDA banned one petroleum-based dye, Red 3, because some studies suggested it caused cancer in lab rats. General Mills removed artificial dyes from Trix in 2015 but brought them back two years later, saying U.S. customers missed the bright colors. But pressure from consumers and politicians has grown since then. President Donald Trump’s health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has urged food companies to phase out petroleum-based artificial dyes. Last summer, General Mills signed an agreement with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton saying it would remove synthetic dyes from all its products by the end of 2027. Retailers are also forcing companies to act. Earlier this year, Target said it would stop selling cereals that contain artificial colors by the end of May. Walmart has also said it will remove artificial colors from its store brands by January 2027.

data.title: Sorry, Wall Street. An IPO isn’t on the menu for Panda Express.
data.description: Panda Express is America’s largest Asian restaurant chain. But it’s still privately held — and its founders have no plans to go public, adopt a franchise model or sell the business to a private equity group.
